column11: Shabbat 77b: ‘An outer garment is called levusha, which is an acronym for lo busha, which means no shame, as one who is clothed is no longer ashamed. A beautiful coat is termed golta, which is an acronym for geli ve’eitiv, which means reveal, remove the coat, and only then I will sit, so that the coat will not get dirty. A bed is called purya, an allusion to the fact that people parin veravin, which means procreate, upon it. column11: Avodah Zarah 3b: ‘The Gemara asks: And during the twelve hours of the night, what does God do? The Gemara answers: If you wish, say that the night is similar to the day, i.e., God performs the same activities as in the day. And if you wish, say instead that He rides on his light cherub and flies in eighteen thousand worlds, as it is stated: “The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even [shinan] thousands” (Psalms 68:18). Do not read it as even [shinan], rather read it as: That which are not [she’einan]. Since the minimum of thousands is two thousand, the phrase: That which are not thousands, indicates that two thousand are not present, i.e., the chariots of God are twenty thousand minus two thousand,…’ Context and connection to Sichat Malakhei HaSharet: In Sichat Malakhei HaSharet 3, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and aggadic-halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 3b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and their teaching (Avodah Zarah 3b): by night He rides upon His swift cherub and glides through eighteen thousand worlds, as it is said: "The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the nature of the ministering angels, the spiritual elevation of the righteous above the angels through Torah and self-mastery, and the five soul-worlds developed in Sichat Malakhei HaSharet.
